title: Terms
text: Three keys · Step 1 of 16 Terms ← Home Step 1 of 16 · Terms 2 · Before you begin → Time 10 min Difficulty Easy Steps 12 terms You will need: Nothing, just read The words you need before the work begins. Use these definitions as a reference throughout the guide. No secrets are needed to search. Find a term 12 terms shown. Seed phrase A human-readable backup used to derive wallet keys. Keep it secret. Recovery may also require a passphrase and, for multisig, the wallet configuration. Passphrase An additional secret used with a BIP39 seed phrase to derive a different wallet. The exact value matters: a typo can open a different, empty wallet. It is not the device PIN. Entropy Unpredictable input used to generate keys. Correct dice collection can provide entropy; it does not protect against malicious software that handles the result. BIP39 A specification for encoding entropy and a checksum as a mnemonic and deriving a seed from it, with an optional passphrase. It is more than a word list. Airgap Separation from networks. In this guide, secret-handling sessions use verified offline software. Turning networking off does not prove the computer is free of malware. Hash · file fingerprint A digest used to detect file changes. A match is useful only if the expected value comes from a trustworthy source; an attacker can replace both a file and its published hash. Digital signature A cryptographic check that a file was signed by a particular key and has not changed. Verify the signer’s key fingerprint independently; “Good signature” alone does not identify a trustworthy author. Extended public key · xpub Public information that can derive a branch of wallet addresses. It does not authorize spending on its own, but revealing it can expose wallet activity. Wallet descriptor A description of the scripts and public-key information used by a wallet. A watch-only descriptor is not a signing secret, but it is privacy-sensitive and important for multisig recovery. 2-of-3 multisig A wallet policy requiring signatures from two of three keys. Recovering with two seeds also needs the missing cosigner’s public information and the correct policy. PSBT Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction: a format for carrying transaction details and signatures between wallet software and signers. It can be used with single-signature and multisig wallets. Watch-only wallet A wallet holding public information so it can display addresses and transactions. It cannot sign by itself. Verify its receive addresses against independently trusted wallet details. Try the 2-of-3 quorum demo Choose a capability to set up an example, or select individual keys and the wallet map to see what they enable. Signing keys A B C Locked Wallet map The saved public descriptor contains the information needed to recreate wallet addresses. Signing Needs two keys Watch-only Needs wallet map Full recovery Needs backups Signing Locked · Choose two keys. Wallet recovery Select keys or add the wallet map. Reset all Illustration only. Rebuilding from three original seeds requires the original wallet settings. Verify a known receive address before relying on a rebuilt wallet. Independent verification: two matching tools are not enough if both rely on the same compromised input. Check the source of the data as well as the result. Specifications: BIP39 · PSBT (BIP174) . ← Home Step 1 of 16 2 · Before you begin →

title: Before you begin
text: Three keys · Step 2 of 16 Before you begin ← 1 · Terms Step 2 of 16 · Before you begin 3 · Pick your path → Time 5 min Difficulty Easy Steps 1 worksheet You will need: Pen and paper What are you protecting your Bitcoin from? Two quick questions help you identify your risks. No secret keys or personal information are collected. 1 Choose your concerns ✓ Theft Someone gets access to a backup. ✓ Fire or flood A backup location is destroyed. ✓ Mistakes I lose or record something incorrectly. ✓ Scams Someone tricks me into sharing a secret. ✓ Inheritance My family needs to recover my Bitcoin. 2 Where is your Bitcoin today? On an exchange Someone else controls the keys. Phone or software wallet My keys are on an internet-connected device. Hardware wallet I already use a dedicated signing device. I haven't started I want to begin correctly. Your security priorities Select the risks you want to plan for, then choose where your Bitcoin is today. These choices help you think through risks; they do not automatically determine a safe wallet configuration. Choose your path → Explore wallet risks and tradeoffs One key and a passphrase Simpler to operate, but forgetting or losing the passphrase can permanently prevent recovery. A compromised device or poorly stored backup can still put funds at risk. Keep the passphrase on paper apart from the plate. If someone finds both the seed backup and its passphrase, they may be able to access your funds. Keep them separately and test restoration. One device, one maker. A flawed or tampered device can still fail you. Words and passphrase go into the device itself during recovery, nowhere else. No hardware company will ever ask for your seed phrase. Check the receiving address on the device screen, not only on the computer screen, before you accept coins. The watch-only wallet cannot sign. Spending requires the signing key for the passphrase-protected wallet; recovery requires the seed and the exact passphrase. A replacement compatible device can be used. Three keys (2-of-3 multisig) Separates signing keys across devices or locations, but makes setup and recovery more complicated. Securely preserve the wallet configuration/descriptor and test the recovery procedure. Most steps to get right. A missed step in any key can lock the wallet later. If fewer than two signing keys remain available, you cannot spend, even with the wallet map. Losing the map can also prevent recovery when the missing public-key information cannot be reconstructed. Keep three plates in three places, and keep the encrypted map apart from any single plate. Two signing keys meet the 2-of-3 threshold, but recovery also requires the correct wallet configuration. Keep verified copies of the descriptor and recovery instructions in separate safe locations, and rehearse reconstruction and spending before funding the wallet. No passphrase on the 2-of-3. The protection comes from three keys in three places, not from a passphrase. Practice spend first, and rehearse on testnet if you have not done this before. Savings do not move until the practice spend works. Shut down fully between keys. A key left in memory is a key at risk. Note: One stolen seed being insufficient applies to an appropriately configured 2-of-3 multisig, not all wallets. Multisig does not automatically solve scams, user error, coercion, or inheritance. Test recovery before trusting a wallet with meaningful funds. Never type seed phrases or passphrases into a website, form, or demo. ← 1 · Terms Step 2 of 16 3 · Pick your path →

title: Checklist
text: Three keys · Step 4 of 16 Checklist You will need for offline testing: Complete offline tester ZIP · Website tools only ZIP Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → ← 3 · Pick your path Step 4 of 16 · Checklist 5 · Two boots → Prepare the materials and the recovery plan before creating keys. Private workspace Fair dice with readable faces, a fixed reading order, a numbered recording sheet, and a pen. A workspace without cameras, microphones, or observers recording secrets. Time to stop and investigate any mismatch without rushing. Verified offline setup Prepare the Tails USB and a separate transfer USB. Read Two boots and Check the files before using downloads. Transfer media must never carry signing secrets back online. The kit contains version-pinned instructions. Confirm that each release, signature and hash belong together; do not substitute a newer binary while keeping an old manifest. Compatibility and version reconciliation remain under review. Backup materials Plan durable backups for three independently created signing seeds, one seed per clearly identified backup. Choose locations so one event does not expose or destroy a signing quorum. Choose a backup format you can read and test. Product capacity varies; this guide does not require a particular brand or forbid additional secured copies. Recovery records Preserve a verified public descriptor or compatible wallet-configuration backup containing all three cosigners’ public information, key origins, derivation paths and the 2-of-3 policy. Two seeds alone do not supply the missing cosigner’s public information. Prepare a private location record and instructions a trusted helper can understand. Rehearse with a disposable test wallet before relying on the process for savings. Before proceeding: review how you will recover at least two signing keys and the complete 2-of-3 wallet configuration. title: Two boots
text: Three keys · Step 5 of 16 Two boots ← 4 · Checklist Step 5 of 16 · Two boots 6 · Check the files → Time 45 min Difficulty Careful Steps 4 sections You will need: Everyday computer · Tails USB You will need for offline testing: Complete offline tester ZIP Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → Separate online preparation from offline secret handling. This page explains the session boundaries. Read Check the files and complete verification before installing or running downloaded software. Page order is not permission to skip that check. Limits: Tails and Offline Mode cannot make compromised hardware or firmware trustworthy. Reusing one computer for several keys creates shared risks that a reboot does not remove. Online preparation Download and verify first Follow the official Tails installation instructions for your computer and release. Authenticate the image before writing it. Keep a separate data USB for the specific verified files you need. Do not put seed phrases, raw entropy, private keys, or passphrases on the data USB or in the everyday operating system. Do not create or unlock Persistent Storage for this guide’s temporary secret-handling sessions. Offline session Set the boundary before secrets At the Tails Welcome Screen, enable Offline Mode before starting the desktop. Older instructions may call this networking disabled. Disconnect network cables and do not enable networking during the session. Use only the verified local tools required for the task. A webpage’s “offline” badge is a reminder, not proof of network isolation or a safe computer. One key or three? The one-key path creates one seed. The three-key path uses a separate session for each seed. Do not load multiple signing seeds in one session. Separate sessions reduce accidental mixing; they do not establish independent hardware trust. Transfer boundary Export only what the next step needs When the guide calls for a transfer, export only reviewed public wallet information or the required transaction file. Public descriptors and xpubs expose wallet activity and still need privacy protection. Never copy seeds, raw entropy, private-key exports, or secret-bearing wallet files back to the online computer. Do not assume a file is public because its name says “backup.” Inspect the export type and follow the wallet’s documentation. End the session Power off fully Finish the offline task and shut down Tails completely before another key session. Do not substitute suspend or hibernate. Keep your physical backup private, away from cameras and microphones. Shutdown ends the session; it does not undo a disclosure, erase a file you saved elsewhere, or remove malicious firmware. If isolation or software integrity is in doubt, stop and investigate before using that key. Stop if: verification is incomplete, networking was enabled while a secret was present, a secret was saved to transfer media, or you cannot identify what an export contains. Do not use a real funded wallet for a rehearsal. Official references: Welcome Screen and Offline Mode · Untrusted computer risks . Next, Check the files. Return to these session rules when the later steps require offline work. ← 4 · Checklist Step 5 of 16 6 · Check the files →

title: Check the files
text: Three keys · Step 6 of 16 Check the files ← 5 · Two boots Step 6 of 16 · Check the files 7 · Make three keys → Time About 30 min Approach One file at a time Checks Source · signer · contents Verification files at a glance Interactive controls are unavailable. All guided instructions are shown below. The software download: the file whose contents you check. Checksum list: the expected hashes; authenticate this list before relying on it. Signature: verify it over the named file or checksum list using the authenticated key. Publisher’s public key: confirm its full fingerprint independently. It is not your wallet seed or private key. Start with Guided checks , or explore the files and example outcomes. Diagrams and sample hashes explain the process; this page does not verify your downloads. 01 Guided checks One check at a time 02 Understand the files See what connects 03 Stop or continue? Explore the outcomes Check the files Start here Before you run it, know what you downloaded. A download needs more than a familiar logo. Answer three questions about each file before you use it. example-app.zip Start with one file Have these ready: your download, the project’s current verification instructions, and any verification files those instructions require. Choose a checkpoint to see the action, the reason, and what a pass means. 1 The right source? Find the exact project release. 2 The expected signer? Check the key and signature. 3 The same contents? Match your file to the reference. CHECKPOINT 1 / 3 Start at the project. Match your download. Use the project’s official instructions for your version and operating system. Keep that page open while you check. 1 Confirm the project’s domain through a source you already trust. Avoid ads and unsolicited download links. 2 Choose the release and platform you intend to use. 3 Save the download and its required verification files together. What this establishes You have identified the intended release. You still need the publisher and file-content checks. Follow the release, not the logo Project’s official instructions Confirm you have the right source ↓ select exact version + operating system Your download example-app.zip ↓ collect its required companions Verification files A signature, signed list, or project verifier File names here are examples. Each project supplies its own verification process. HTTPS protects the connection. It does not establish software safety. Next: check the signer → CHECKPOINT 2 / 3 Make sure the signature belongs to the right key. Use the publisher’s public verification key . This is separate from your wallet keys: file verification never needs your seed words or private keys. Establish whose key you expect, then check what it signed. 1 Follow the publisher’s documented process to confirm the signing key’s full fingerprint using an independently trusted source. 2 Use the project’s verifier or documented signature commands for the exact release. 3 Confirm the signature covers your download directly, or the checksum list that names your file. What this establishes A valid signature connects the signed content to the authenticated signing key. It does not audit the program’s code. Two checks that belong together Expected publisher’s key Full fingerprint independently confirmed ↓ use this key to verify Signature checks out For the download or its checksum list ↓ now you can use Authenticated signed content Compare the named file if a list was signed “Good signature” + unknown key is incomplete. A new key or unexplained fingerprint change needs investigation. No signature available? Use the publisher’s documented alternative. Do not treat an unsigned hash as publisher proof. Next: check your copy → CHECKPOINT 3 / 3 Compare your file with the expected hash. A SHA-256 hash is a 64-character digest of a file’s contents. Calculate yours and compare all 64 characters with the authenticated reference for that exact file. Windows macOS Linux Get-FileHash -LiteralPath ".\example-app.zip" -Algorithm SHA256 | Format-List PowerShell · run in the file’s folder, or use its full path Copy command What a match means Your file matches the referenced bytes. If the reference itself is unauthenticated, a match alone does not establish who published the file. If the publisher signs the download directly, follow its documented direct-signature process. A separate checksum list may not be required. Illustration only Show a mismatch Authenticated expected hash 9f3a18c7d42e6b508a9174c3e65f20b77dc58a014b2e939f6a70d1c84e5b6230 Calculated hash of your copy 9f3a18c7d42e6b508a9174c3e65f20b77dc58a014b2e939f6a70d1c84e5b6230 All 64 characters match These values are made-up teaching examples, not a checksum for a real download. Keep a record: filename, release, full hash, method, and key fingerprint where applicable. Explore stop / continue → Stop when something is unexplained. A wrong hash, failed signature, unknown key, or uncertain release needs investigation before you run the file. What if a signature checker reports an untrusted key? A valid signature and local key-trust settings answer different questions. “Not certified” may reflect your local trust configuration, but you still need to independently establish the key’s identity. Investigate an unexpected key, bad signature, or unresolved warning. Check the files · explain the pieces File roles Four files. Different jobs. The extra downloads can feel like clutter until you see what each one does. This example follows a project that publishes a signed checksum list. One release folder · select a file below to understand its role A example-app.zip The software you intend to use. B SHA256SUMS The expected hash for each release file. C SHA256SUMS.asc The signature for that checksum list. D publisher-key.asc The public key used to check the signature. This is the download you are checking. Calculate a hash from this file’s contents. Match it to the entry for this exact filename in the authenticated checksum list. What this file does not tell you Its name, icon, and successful download do not prove who published it. How the evidence connects Signed-list example 1 · Establish the reference Authenticated publisher key + Signature + checksum list ↓ Verify the signature over the list Expected hash from an authenticated list Confirm the key fingerprint independently first. 2 · Examine your copy Your downloaded example-app.zip + A SHA-256 calculation tool ↓ Calculate the digest of your copy Calculated hash for the downloaded file Use a trusted tool, following the project’s instructions. AUTHENTICATED EXPECTED HASH ↔ YOUR CALCULATED HASH Same filename. Same release. Every character. A full match links your copy to the authenticated reference. A mismatch means stop and investigate. Some projects sign the download directly. In that case, verify the signature over the downloaded file using the authenticated key. Use the publisher’s actual filenames and instructions; the four filenames above are examples. Check the files · see the outcome Example outcomes Know when to stop. Know what to do next. Explore four sample results. The decision map shows exactly where a verification attempt needs more work. Everything lines up All checks established Only the hash matches Reference not authenticated “Good signature” Signer’s identity unknown One character differs Calculated hash mismatch Example verification path 1 Right source, file, and release? YES · continue ↓ 2 Expected key identity established? YES · continue ↓ 3 Signature over the list valid? YES · continue ↓ 4 Your file’s hash matches its entry? YES · continue ↓ RECORD THE FILE-CHECK RESULT Selected scenario The file checks line up. You identified the release, independently authenticated the publisher key, verified its signature on the checksum list, and matched the entire hash for your file. File checks complete for this example Record what you checked. This establishes the file’s connection to the authenticated release reference. What you do next Keep the filename, release, full hash, method, and key fingerprint in your verification record. Continue only when the guide’s other release and testing requirements are also satisfied. This map illustrates a signed checksum list. A project’s direct-file signature or dedicated verification tool may use a different route. A successful file check does not establish that software is bug-free or approved for custody. Current instructions always come from the project: Tails installation ↗ Sparrow verification ↗ Public test site: the tools and instructions remain under review. Never enter signing secrets into the live website. Successful file checks do not certify software safety or approve a custody release. Testing Plebum Dominium’s own downloads? For public-fixture testing: use the manifest and instructions supplied with your exact package version. You will need for offline testing: Fingerprint checker · ZIP checksums Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → A package checksum checks consistency with its reference; it does not independently audit code or establish publisher identity. Review and authenticate any verification script before running it. Keep a verification record: release, exact filename, full hash, method, and signing-key fingerprint when applicable. Verify every required file before beginning your path’s offline secret-handling session. ← 5 · Two boots Step 6 of 16 7 · Make three keys →

title: Make three keys
text: Three keys · Step 7 of 16 Make the three keys ← 6 · Check the files Step 7 of 16 · Make three keys 8 · Build the 2-of-3 → Time 30-45 min Difficulty Moderate Steps 6 sections You will need: 5 dice · Paper and pen · The worksheet You will need for offline testing: Dice converter HTML · Python dice converter Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → You will roll dice to create three separate Bitcoin seed phrases. Each one becomes 24 words. The computer never sees the network while you work. Safety first: Never enter seed words on an online computer. Boot Tails with networking Disabled before you start. Shut down fully between each key. What you will do Boot Tails offline. Copy the dice converter page. Roll dice. Enter the faces. The page counts to 256 bits. Write down the 24 words. Prove them with a second tool. Repeat for Seed 2 and Seed 3, with a full shutdown between each. Step 1 / 6 Boot Tails. Copy the converter. Boot Tails with networking set to Disabled. Copy the checked dice converter page from the data USB to the Desktop. Check: Open only the verified local copy after enabling Tails Offline Mode. An offline indicator alone does not prove network isolation. If it reports online, stop. Step 2 / 6 Roll the dice. Enter the faces. Roll five dice at once. Enter each face as you roll it. Using fair, independently rolled dice and a fixed reading order, faces 1 to 4 count as bits (1=00, 2=01, 3=10, 4=11). Faces 5 and 6 are skipped, roll those dice again. The page counts the pairs and stops you at 128. SHAKE 1 SHAKE 2 SHAKE 3 11 RE-ROLL 01 00 10 01 01 RE-ROLL 11 11 00 10 00 10 RE-ROLL 00 01 RE-ROLL 10 256-BIT STRING 11 00 10 01 01 01 11 00 10 11 00 10 00 01 10 …keep rolling… 256 / 256 BITS 10 / 256 20 / 256 30 / 256 256 / 256 24 WORDS Roll as many times as needed to get 256 bits of entropy: about 39 shakes. Check: The page shows 128 pairs and 256 bits. Count accepted pairs, not an estimated number of shakes. Step 3 / 6 Write the 24 words. At 256 bits the page prints 24 words. In a 24-word BIP39 phrase, the last word contains three entropy bits and eight checksum bits. It is not an arbitrary check word: never invent or alter it. Write all 24 on the grid. Compare them privately in order, away from cameras and microphones. Check: All 24 words and their positions are recorded accurately; a valid checksum does not prove safe randomness. Step 4 / 6 Prove it with a second tool. Use a separately verified offline implementation with the exact same 256-bit entropy and BIP39 settings. Raw dice inputs are not interchangeable between tools: some hash the roll string while this guide maps accepted faces to bit pairs. Confirm the input method before comparing all 24 words. If you cannot establish that the inputs and method match, stop; do not guess or choose a preferred output. Check: Both tools show the same 24 words. Step 5 / 6 Shut down. Start the next key. Shut Tails down fully. Wait until the screen is dark. Then boot again for Seed 2. New rolls, new words. Repeat for Seed 3. Never continue a list from the previous boot. Check: Each seed has its own 24 words on its own grid. Three grids total. Step 6 / 6 Confirm the checks agree. The checksum detects many transcription errors, but not all of them. It does not authenticate the source of the words. At least two checks must agree: the two tools showing the same words, and the wallet (Sparrow or Electrum, offline) opening the list without error. If anything disagrees, stop. Stop if: The page says online. The two tools show different words. The wallet rejects the list. Any of these means stop and start that key over. Next, Build the 2-of-3. ← 6 · Check the files Step 7 of 16 8 · Build the 2-of-3 →

title: Build the 2-of-3
text: Three keys · Step 8 of 16 Build the 2-of-3 ← 7 · Make three keys Step 8 of 16 · Build the 2-of-3 9 · Practice spend → Time 45-60 min Difficulty Careful Steps 7 steps You will need: The three paper keys · Verified Sparrow You will need for offline testing: 2-of-3 demo Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → The final watch-only wallet is built from three public keys. Earlier steps use one seed per offline boot to obtain each public key. What comes out is the wallet map, which can watch the money and never spend it. Safety first: Never enter seed words on an online computer. You will boot Tails four times: once per seed to copy its public key, then once more with no seed to build the vault. Files used: Sparrow 2.5.5. Tails 7.16 or later 7.x (verified). Electrum 4.8.3 for the cross-check. What you will do Boot Tails offline. Launch Sparrow from the terminal. Extract each seed's public key, one per boot. Build the 2-of-3 vault with no seed. Export the map. Independently verify the cosigners and wallet policy, then compare several receiving addresses. Step 1 / 7 Boot Tails. Networking stays off. The entire sheet happens with networking Disabled. Check it on every boot. Step 2 / 7 Open the terminal. Launch Sparrow. Run these commands one at a time. Wait for each command to finish before entering the next. The shell prompt is not part of a command. cd ~/Desktop tar -xvf sparrowwallet-2.5.5-x86_64.tar.gz cd Sparrow ./bin/Sparrow Sparrow may take 15 to 30 seconds to open. The terminal may remain occupied while Sparrow runs. If a command reports an error or the expected window does not open, stop and investigate; text color alone is not an error check. Step 3 / 7 New wallet: 2 of 3, native Segwit. File → New Wallet. Pick Multi Signature, Native Segwit, 2 of 3. The path must read m/48'/0'/0'/2' . Anything else: stop. Check: The path reads exactly m/48'/0'/0'/2' . Step 4 / 7 Keystore 1: Seed 1 in, public key out. Keystore 1 → New or Imported Software Wallet → type Seed 1's 24 words. Export the xpub. Save it to the data USB as s1-xpub.txt . Close Sparrow. Shut down. Wait for a dark screen. Step 5 / 7 Twice more. One seed per boot. Boot again for Seed 2 → s2-xpub.txt . Shut down. Boot again for Seed 3 → s3-xpub.txt . Shut down. Check: Three xpub files on the USB. One seed per boot, never two. Step 6 / 7 Fresh boot. No seed. Build the vault. Boot Tails again. Do not type any seed. New wallet → Multi Signature → Native Segwit → 2 of 3 → import the three xpub files. Confirm the path. Export the output descriptor to the data USB. That file is the wallet map. Try the 2-of-3 demo → Why keep the descriptor and all three seed backups? Lost a seed plate? Two seeds + the wallet map. The verified descriptor supplies the missing signer’s public key. The two surviving keys can sign. Lost the wallet map? All three seeds + the original setup. The third seed supplies the missing public key, so you can rebuild the descriptor without the saved file. Spending still takes two signatures. Step 7 / 7 · Before funding Verify the wallet independently Matching addresses alone cannot prove a coordinator is honest if both devices use the same unverified descriptor. 01 · Record addresses Record several complete receiving addresses from Sparrow offline. Write the full strings, not just QR codes. 02 · Verify each cosigner On a separate trusted offline device, compare each cosigner’s master fingerprint, derivation path, and extended public key with records obtained directly from that signer—not solely from the coordinator. 03 · Check the wallet policy Confirm the 2-of-3 threshold, native SegWit script type, and full descriptor including key order and checksum where supported. 04 · Rebuild and compare Reconstruct a watch-only wallet from independently verified details. Compare several receiving addresses character for character. Never enter seeds on a networked device. Stop before funding if anything differs. If a key, fingerprint, path, policy, or address differs, investigate offline. Two devices using the same substituted descriptor may show matching attacker-controlled addresses. Next, Practice spend. ← 7 · Make three keys Step 8 of 16 9 · Practice spend →

title: Practice spend
text: Three keys · Step 9 of 16 Practice spend ← 8 · Build the 2-of-3 Step 9 of 16 · Practice spend 10 · Metal and the map → Practice the complete transaction before relying on it. Prepare a disposable rehearsal Use the testnet rehearsal first, with three disposable keys and a verified 2-of-3 wallet configuration. Never use a funded wallet’s seeds for a practice exercise. A successful practice spend is not a full recovery audit. Keep the online coordinator watch-only. Each signer needs the correct wallet policy and relevant key information; restoring a seed alone does not establish the intended multisig wallet. Follow the documented setup for your particular signer. 1. Build and inspect In the online watch-only wallet, choose the destination, amount and fee, then export the unsigned PSBT. Record the intended payment using destination information obtained independently from the recipient, not just copied from the coordinator display. A PSBT carries transaction and signing information. It is not a seed backup and can expose financial metadata. Transfer only the intended transaction file, never a wallet containing private keys. 2. Verify before the first signature On the first trusted signer, check the network, wallet policy, full recipient address, amount and total fee. Account for every output: any change must return to the verified wallet. Stop if the signer cannot identify change or explain an output. Use the signer’s documented transaction review. Paper notes help compare intent but do not make a compromised computer trustworthy. For the Tails software-signing workflow, start in Offline Mode and load only this signer’s secret. Export the partially signed PSBT, then fully shut down. 3. Review again with the second signer Use a different key belonging to the same verified 2-of-3 wallet. Review the same transaction independently, including all outputs and the fee, before signing. A file name or signature count alone is not verification. For software signing, use a fresh offline session. Rebooting the same computer does not provide independent hardware or remove a firmware compromise. Do not collect both seeds in the online coordinator or one saved wallet file. 4. Finalize and broadcast Return the signed PSBT to the online coordinator, finalize it when the required signatures are present for every input, and review the resulting transaction before broadcasting. Watch for confirmation on the selected network. If any field changes unexpectedly, stop and investigate. Do not sign a replacement you have not reviewed. Record what worked and rehearse recovery separately before funding a real setup. Pause and check: Stop if the wallet policy is uncertain, an output is unexplained, a fee is unexpected, or a signing secret reaches an online environment. ← 8 · Build the 2-of-3 Step 9 of 16 10 · Metal and the map →

title: Metal and the map
text: Three keys · Step 10 of 16 Metal and the map ← 9 · Practice spend Step 10 of 16 · Metal and the map 11 · Rehearse on testnet → Make a durable backup without losing the ability to recover. Record accurately Back up each of the three seeds separately using the chosen medium’s instructions. Preserve word order and any required encoding information. Work privately and compare every entry against the original. Keep the original protected while checking the replacement. A damaged or ambiguous mark needs correction before you rely on it. Check recovery safely Use the wallet’s documented backup-check or recovery procedure on trusted equipment. Do not wipe your only working signer to test an unproven backup. Never type seeds into this website or an online form. For a rehearsal, use a disposable test wallet. For an existing funded wallet, plan the verification carefully before changing devices or backups. Keep the complete recovery information Preserve a verified public descriptor or compatible wallet-configuration backup containing all three cosigners’ public information, key origins, derivation paths and the 2-of-3 policy. Two seeds alone do not supply the missing cosigner’s public information. Lost a seed plate? Two seeds + the wallet map. The verified descriptor supplies the missing signer’s public key. The two surviving keys can sign. Lost the wallet map? All three seeds + the original setup. The third seed supplies the missing public key, so you can rebuild the descriptor without the saved file. Spending still takes two signatures. Rehearse both scenarios with a disposable test wallet and verify that each rebuild reproduces a known receive address. Try the 2-of-3 demo → A public-only descriptor cannot sign by itself, but it reveals wallet information. Confirm that the export contains no private keys before treating it as public data. Protect its availability and privacy. Plan copies and locations Balance loss, theft, access, and disaster risks. More copies can improve availability and also expose secrets in more places. Document which locations contain which material; do not combine enough signing secrets in one place to defeat your separation plan. Do not destroy an original merely because a new backup looks correct. Retire it only after a successful recovery check and a deliberate review of the remaining copies. Revisit the plan when locations or helpers change. Stop if: a backup is unreadable, the recovered wallet differs, or any required passphrase or configuration is missing. Do not overwrite or discard the remaining working material. ← 9 · Practice spend Step 10 of 16 11 · Rehearse on testnet →

title: Rehearse on testnet
text: Three keys · Step 11 of 16 Rehearse on testnet ← 10 · Metal and the map Step 11 of 16 · Rehearse on testnet 12 · Protect the wallet map → Learn with disposable keys and test coins, then rehearse recovery too. 1. Select the test network Sparrow documents Tools → Restart in Testnet . Confirm the network shown by your installed version, and use a server, faucet and explorer for that same network. Different test networks are not interchangeable. Test coins are for practice. Do not send real bitcoin, pay for test coins, or give a faucet seed words or a passphrase. A faucet needs only the intended public receive address. Interfaces and services can differ from mainnet. 2. Build a separate practice wallet Create three new disposable keys and a test-only 2-of-3 wallet. Label all records TEST ONLY. Keep the configuration and temporary test backups long enough to complete the recovery exercise. Never reuse these keys for real funds. Verify the threshold, script type, all three cosigner public keys and their origins against independent signer records. A matching receive address alone does not prove the coordinator is trustworthy. 3. Receive, review and sign Receive test coins at an address verified against the intended wallet, wait for confirmation, then follow Practice spend . Review destination, amount, fee and change before each signature. Broadcast on the same test network. A confirmation shows that transaction was accepted; it does not prove every backup or signer combination works. 4. Recover from the test backups Reconstruct the disposable wallet from its saved configuration and test backups in a separate test environment. Check its policy and transaction history, then rehearse spending using each intended pair of signers. Do not wipe a real working wallet. Record failures and resolve them before committing real funds. Keep test records clearly separated while learning; when finished, retire the disposable wallet and its records. Never promote a test seed into a mainnet backup. Pause and check: Stop if the network is unclear, you are using real wallet secrets, or recovery depends on missing configuration. This rehearsal can be done before funding even though the guide introduces backup concepts earlier. ← 10 · Metal and the map Step 11 of 16 12 · Protect the wallet map →

title: Protect the wallet map
text: Three keys · Step 12 of 16 Hide the wallet map You will need for offline testing: Wallet-map tool HTML · Python wallet-map tool Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → ← 11 · Rehearse on testnet Step 12 of 16 · Protect the wallet map 13 · If I am gone → Protect the wallet map’s privacy without making recovery depend on an untested file. Understand the map A verified public-only descriptor describes the wallet’s scripts, cosigner public keys and derivation information. It can reveal wallet activity but cannot sign by itself. Some exports contain private keys: confirm the export type before treating it as public data. Keep the complete verified configuration. Do not assume three seeds alone automatically recover every script type, derivation path or wallet setting. Encryption protects confidentiality; it does not replace configuration backups. Choose a recoverable protection plan Decide who needs access after loss or incapacity. Keep more than one protected copy, with a durable record of the decryption method and its password or required key. Avoid making every copy depend on one forgotten password. The file-encryption password is separate from a Bitcoin wallet passphrase and a device PIN. Do not reuse signing secrets as encryption passwords. Arrange separate access to encrypted copies and their unlocking material without making either impossible for your recovery plan. Encrypt offline using a documented method Tails includes Kleopatra: select Sign/Encrypt , choose the file, then Encrypt with password for password-based encryption. Use Decrypt/Verify to open the encrypted file. Follow the official Tails instructions for your installed version. Use an offline session and trusted software. Never enter a real encryption password, private key or seed on this hosted website. A browser’s offline indicator is not proof that the system is isolated. Verify before replacing any copy Start with harmless sample text. Test decryption in a later session, using the exact software intended for recovery. For a real map, verify the entire recovered contents against the original before relying on the encrypted copy. Keep the existing protected backup until these checks pass. Deleting a file or emptying the trash does not prove every copy has been erased. Plan plaintext handling before writing sensitive material to persistent storage. Keep the existing tool in review The bundled descriptor tool remains available, but its cross-tool compatibility and offline behavior still need independent testing in this review. Do not use it as your only recovery path or assume its self-reported checks certify it. No encryption implementation has been changed here. Rehearse with non-sensitive sample data and retain a verified recovery option. The legacy print packet has not yet been reconciled with this guidance. Pause and check: Stop if decryption fails, the recovered map differs, the export contains unexpected private material, or you cannot explain how a trusted helper would regain access. ← 11 · Rehearse on testnet Step 12 of 16 13 · If I am gone →

title: If I am gone
text: Three keys · Step 13 of 16 If I am gone ← 12 · Protect the wallet map Step 13 of 16 · If I am gone 14 · If you get stuck → Help a trusted person understand what to find—and when to stop. Leave a clear private plan Describe the wallet type, the location of the full instructions, the required recovery items, and a trusted contact who can explain the process. Keep signing secrets out of this website, email, and the general instruction sheet. Separate ownership and access arrangements from the technical recovery instructions. Make sure the intended person can find the plan when needed. Identify the required items This path requires at least two signing keys and the complete 2-of-3 wallet configuration. Preserve a verified public descriptor or compatible wallet-configuration backup containing all three cosigners’ public information, key origins, derivation paths and the 2-of-3 policy. Two seeds alone do not supply the missing cosigner’s public information. Keep each signing seed on a separate compatible signer during the planned hardware-wallet recovery. Do not assume an arbitrary replacement device supports the recorded policy. Check compatibility before importing secrets. Confirm the recovered wallet Follow the recorded, rehearsed procedure and verify the policy and wallet details against independent trusted records. An address match alone does not establish that a coordinator is trustworthy. If the wallet is empty or differs from the records, stop. Check the passphrase, account, network, derivation information and synchronization before concluding funds are lost. Do not overwrite backups or create replacement keys as a guess. Practice before an emergency Walk through locating the records and explaining the steps with the intended helper. Use a disposable test wallet for hands-on training, without exposing the owner’s signing secrets. When a legitimate recovery is needed, independently verify the destination and transaction details on trusted signing equipment. A small successful transfer is useful evidence, but it is not a complete audit of the recovery setup. Protect the secrets: no legitimate support agent needs a seed phrase or private key. If the instructions, equipment compatibility, or wallet identity are uncertain, stop before entering secrets or signing. ← 12 · Protect the wallet map Step 13 of 16 14 · If you get stuck →

title: If you get stuck
text: Three keys · Step 14 of 16 If you get stuck ← 13 · If I am gone Step 14 of 16 · If you get stuck 15 · Tough questions → Find the problem, preserve what still works, and stop when the next step is uncertain. What setup is this? A 2-of-3 wallet uses three distinct signing keys; any two can authorize a spend under the correct wallet policy. What recovery information matters? Keep the complete wallet configuration and all three cosigner public records as well as the signing backups. Losing two signing keys can prevent spending; losing configuration is a separate recovery problem. Three seeds do not guarantee automatic reconstruction. The download or version does not match Stop before running it. Confirm the exact release, file, signature and full hash from the intended publisher. Do not assume a newer release is compatible or an older release is safe. The staging download inventory has unresolved mismatches; see Downloads . The two converters disagree Preserve the original rolls privately. Check transcription, input method, bit order and settings. Do not guess a replacement word or choose whichever output you prefer. Use public test vectors before trusting the procedure; funded-wallet backups must not be edited to make a check pass. The restored wallet looks empty Stop before wiping or discarding anything. Check the network, account, script type, derivation settings, passphrase if used, and synchronization. Preserve working devices and backups while investigating. Never send secrets to someone offering recovery help. Where should secrets be kept? Keep signing secrets offline and protected from theft and loss. Avoid photographs, email, cloud notes and online forms. Plan durable copies and separate locations, then test recovery. A location card is not a substitute for the backups. How can a helper prepare? Practice with a disposable wallet and a private written plan. Use the recovery planning guide where it matches your wallet. Never paste real seeds, passwords or passphrases into this site. ← 13 · If I am gone Step 14 of 16 15 · Tough questions →

title: Tough questions
text: Three keys · Step 15 of 16 Tough questions ← 14 · If you get stuck Step 15 of 16 · Tough questions 16 · Recovery card → Understand what the design protects—and what still depends on your equipment and recovery plan. Does a fresh boot remove every risk? No. Offline sessions reduce network exposure but do not establish trustworthy hardware or firmware. A persistent compromise can observe keys across different boots on the same computer. One key per boot is not independent hardware isolation. Are dice automatically trustworthy? The input must be unpredictable and the conversion correct. Biased rolls, transcription errors or incompatible input methods undermine the result. Observable dice do not eliminate trust in the software that turns rolls into keys. Can one stolen key spend? One distinct key cannot satisfy a correctly configured 2-of-3 policy alone. Two compromised signing keys can. Devices containing copies of the same key do not create independent cosigners. Can I recreate the map from seeds? Do not rely on that as the backup plan. Preserve verified configuration, including script type, key origins and all cosigner public information. Protect its privacy and test that it restores the intended wallet. Should every cosigner have a passphrase? A cosigner passphrase adds a recovery dependency. This guide’s basic three-key route does not require one. Adding any requires documenting exactly which signer uses it and testing the resulting configuration; it is not a substitute for key separation. What proves the plan works? Rehearse setup, signing and recovery with disposable test keys, including the intended signer pairs. A matching receive address or a single successful payment is useful evidence, not proof that a coordinator is trustworthy or every backup works. ← 14 · If you get stuck Step 15 of 16 16 · Recovery card →

title: Recovery card
text: Three keys · Step 16 of 16 Recovery card ← 15 · Tough questions Step 16 of 16 · Recovery card Review this path → A private pointer to your recovery plan—not a wallet backup. What this card is for A short location record helps an authorized person find the complete instructions and required materials. It cannot replace at least two signing keys and the complete 2-of-3 wallet configuration. Location information can help a thief too. Protect the card even though it contains no signing secrets. Write these pointers offline Wallet type: 2-of-3 multisig. Where to find the complete recovery instructions. Separate seed-backup locations and wallet-configuration location. Trusted contact and date last reviewed. Location of any separate decryption instructions, if required. Write privately on paper. This page intentionally provides no form for entering real locations or secrets. Never include these No seed words, raw entropy, private keys, wallet passphrases, or decryption passwords on the card. Keep it separate from the materials it points to. A descriptor can contain private keys; only a verified public-only export belongs in the non-signing configuration records. Keep it current Check that the intended person can follow the pointers. Update the record after moving a backup or changing the recovery plan, then account for obsolete copies. The downloadable legacy card/PDF has not yet been reconciled with these revised instructions. Do not treat that older packet as a verified version of this page. Recovery still requires verification: use the complete, rehearsed procedure. A list of locations, a device brand, or a derivation-path label is not sufficient by itself. ← 15 · Tough questions Step 16 of 16 Review this path →
